name: LangChain
purpose: Framework for building applications with language models, providing abstractions over model providers, prompts, output parsing, retrieval, tools and chains, with a very large integration ecosystem.
journalism_use_case: Provider-independent plumbing for newsroom AI features: write a claim-extraction or classification step once and run it against a local model via llama.cpp today and a different model next year, without rewriting the application around a provider's SDK.
pros: Provider abstraction has real strategic value for a newsroom: it makes 'we can move off this model' true in practice, which matters when a provider changes terms or you move work in-house for privacy
The integration ecosystem is unmatched, so connecting to an unusual document store, model or tool is usually already done
MIT licensed with a 1.x line (langchain-core 1.8.1, 2026-11-15) and enormous community (149,770 stars), so there is abundant material to learn from
Reached a stable major version, which materially reduces the API churn that characterised its earlier history
cons: Abstraction cost is real and widely felt: debugging a chain means reading through layers of framework code, and for simple tasks a direct API call is clearer and more maintainable
Historically severe API churn, and while 1.x has stabilised, a large body of tutorials and code targets incompatible earlier versions — which makes learning from examples hazardous
Commercial company with a hosted observability and deployment platform (LangSmith), so the convenient path toward production involves a paid service
Breadth encourages building complex agentic systems where a simple prompt would do, and complexity in a journalism tool is a reliability liability
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 149,770 stars, release langchain-core==1.8.1 (2026-11-15), pushed 2026-11-17, MIT licence. The API-churn history is documented in the project's own migration guides across major versions and is a widely discussed characteristic.
assessment: Use it for the provider-abstraction benefit and resist its gravitational pull toward complexity — for most newsroom tasks (summarise, extract claims, classify) a direct call to your local model with a well-tested prompt is more maintainable and easier to explain than a chain. For your profile the specific value is insulation from provider lock-in; the specific risk is building an agentic system whose behaviour nobody can account for when an editor asks how a figure was produced.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release langchain-core==1.8.1 (2026-11-15), 149,770 stars, MIT licence. Same-day commits and continuous releases across a monorepo of packages, under well-funded commercial maintenance.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the framework; models and services you connect carry their own terms.
licence_restrictions: Framework unrestricted. LangSmith and LangGraph Platform are separate commercial services.
costs: Framework free. Costs are the models you call — local GPU infrastructure or hosted per-token charges (not priced here). LangSmith observability is a paid service. Estimate.
privacy: Depends entirely on configuration: pointed at a local model it is fully private, pointed at a hosted provider it sends your content there. The framework makes switching easy, which is both its value and the configuration risk.
alternatives: Direct calls to an OpenAI-compatible local endpoint, which for simple tasks is clearer
Haystack for a more explicit pipeline model aimed at search and RAG
simonw/llm for a CLI-first approach to the same provider abstraction

name: LangGraph
purpose: Library for building stateful, multi-step language-model applications as explicit graphs with persistence, human-in-the-loop interrupts, checkpointing and streaming.
journalism_use_case: Research-agent workflows where a human must be able to intervene: a multi-step document-analysis process that pauses for a reporter to approve or correct an intermediate conclusion before continuing — which is the only responsible shape for an agentic system in journalism.
pros: Human-in-the-loop interrupts are first-class rather than bolted on, which is precisely the control journalism needs: the system stops and asks rather than proceeding on a wrong inference
Explicit graph structure and checkpointing make a multi-step process inspectable and resumable, so you can audit what the system did at each step — essential if its output informs a story
MIT licensed with very active development (1.2.22, 2026-11-14; pushed 2026-11-17) and strong adoption (45,068 stars)
State persistence means a long-running analysis survives interruption, which matters for corpus-scale work
cons: Agentic complexity is the central risk: a graph with several model-driven decision points is hard to explain and hard to test, and journalism needs explicable processes more than capable ones
Inherits LangChain's ecosystem and company, including the paid platform for deployment and observability — so the production path leads toward a commercial service
Building reliable agents requires substantial evaluation work the framework does not do, and the gap between a working demo and a trustworthy tool is large
Rapid development pace means pinning is necessary and patterns change between versions
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 45,068 stars with release 1.2.22 (2026-11-14), pushed 2026-11-17, MIT licence. Strong adoption is clear from the metrics; the agentic-reliability concern is a general property of the approach rather than a defect of this implementation.
assessment: Pilot it for one well-scoped workflow with mandatory human checkpoints — for example a document-triage process that proposes classifications a reporter confirms. For your profile the governing principle should be that an agent may gather and propose but never conclude: every published claim traces to a human decision with the evidence in front of them. Used that way LangGraph's interrupt model is genuinely useful; used to automate judgement it is a liability.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 1.2.22 (2026-11-14), 45,068 stars, MIT licence. Same-day commits and frequent releases under commercial maintenance.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the framework; models carry their own terms.
licence_restrictions: Framework unrestricted. LangGraph Platform is a separate commercial offering.
costs: Framework free. Model inference is the cost — multi-step agents multiply token or GPU consumption per task, often by an order of magnitude over a single call, which is easy to underestimate. Estimate.
privacy: Configuration-dependent as with LangChain: local models keep everything internal, hosted providers do not. Checkpointed state persists intermediate content, so the state store needs the same protection as the source documents.
alternatives: smolagents for a much smaller agent framework with less machinery
A plain scripted pipeline with explicit human review steps, which is often sufficient and always clearer
Haystack pipelines where the task is retrieval rather than multi-step reasoning

name: smolagents
purpose: Minimal agent library where agents write and execute code to use tools, with a small core, support for many model backends and sandboxed execution options.
journalism_use_case: A deliberately small agent framework for research tasks: give a model a few tools (search your archive, fetch a page, run a calculation) and let it chain them, with little enough machinery that you can read the whole framework and understand what it did.
pros: Minimal by design, so the framework is readable in an afternoon — which matters enormously when you must explain to an editor how an AI-assisted finding was produced
Code-writing agents are a powerful pattern for data work: the agent can compute rather than guess, and the code it wrote is an auditable artefact
Apache-2.0 from Hugging Face with strong adoption (30,404 stars) and active development (pushed 2026-11-17)
Backend-agnostic, so it runs against a local model via llama.cpp or vLLM without modification
cons: Code-executing agents are a serious security consideration: an agent that writes and runs code on your infrastructure, with access to your archive, is an attack surface and needs sandboxing that the library supports but does not force
Release cadence is uneven: v1.26.0 dates from 2026-05-29 against commits in November 2026, so the published release lags development considerably
Minimalism means you build the guardrails: rate limits, tool permissions, output validation and human checkpoints are yours to add
Agent reliability remains the fundamental issue — a code-writing agent can produce confidently wrong analysis, and the code it wrote looks authoritative
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 30,404 stars with release v1.26.0 (2026-05-29) against a push on 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0. The release-versus-commit gap is visible in the API data.
assessment: The agent framework I would choose for your context, specifically because you can read it — explicability is worth more than capability in a newsroom tool. Two non-negotiables if you deploy it: sandbox code execution properly (container with no network and no access to source material unless explicitly mounted), and treat agent-written code as an artefact to review, since it is simultaneously the method and the thing that could be wrong. Pin to a commit given the release lag.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.26.0 (2026-05-29), 30,404 stars, Apache-2.0. Same-day commits with a release nearly six months old — active development, lagging release engineering.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the library; models carry their own terms.
costs: Library free. Model inference costs apply and agent loops multiply them. Sandboxing infrastructure (containers or a dedicated VM) is a modest additional cost. Estimate.
privacy: Local-model configuration keeps content internal. The sharper risk is the agent's own access: an agent with tools that read your archive and fetch URLs could exfiltrate content through a crafted request, so network egress from the sandbox should be denied by default.
alternatives: LangGraph where explicit state machines and human interrupts are needed
A scripted pipeline with no agent, which for most tasks is sufficient and fully predictable
OpenHands or similar for software-engineering agents rather than research tasks
blockers: Code-executing agents require deliberate sandboxing and egress denial before touching source material

name: llm (Simon Willison's CLI)
purpose: Command-line tool and Python library for interacting with language models — local and remote — with a plugin system, prompt templates, logging of every prompt and response to SQLite, and piping into shell workflows.
journalism_use_case: Scriptable AI in a shell pipeline with an audit trail: pipe a document into a model, get structured output, and have every prompt and response automatically logged to SQLite — which means an AI-assisted analysis has a complete, queryable record of exactly what was asked and answered.
pros: Automatic SQLite logging of every prompt and response is the standout feature for journalism: it gives you a provenance record of AI use without any discipline required from the user, and you can query it later with Datasette
Shell-pipeline design composes with the rest of a Unix toolkit, so AI becomes one step in a pipeline rather than a separate application
Apache-2.0 with very active maintenance (0.37.3, 2026-11-16; pushed 2026-11-17) and a plugin ecosystem covering local models (llama.cpp, Ollama) and hosted providers
Prompt templates make a repeatable extraction task into a saved, version-controllable artefact
cons: CLI-first, so it serves engineers and terminal-comfortable analysts rather than reporters

The logging database accumulates the full content of every prompt — which for source documents means a second copy of sensitive material in an easily overlooked location that needs the same protection as the originals
Plugin quality varies, and model-specific features are exposed unevenly across providers
Single-maintainer project, though with an exceptional track record of long-term care
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 12,769 stars, release 0.37.3 (2026-11-16), pushed 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0. The prompt-logging design is documented by the maintainer and is unusual among LLM tools.
assessment: Adopt it as the standard way your team invokes models from a shell, largely for the audit trail — being able to show exactly which prompt produced a figure is the difference between an explicable method and an assertion. For your profile there is one control to apply immediately: the logs database contains full document content, so put it on encrypted storage with the same access restrictions as your source material, and set a retention policy. People forget it exists.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 0.37.3 (2026-11-16), 12,769 stars, Apache-2.0. Same-day commits and a release within a day of the survey, from a maintainer with a long record of sustained project care.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the tool; models and providers carry their own terms.
costs: Tool free. Model costs depend on the backend — local inference on your GPU, or hosted per-token charges (not priced here). Negligible tool overhead.
privacy: Depends on the configured model: local plugins keep everything internal, hosted providers do not. The specific privacy item to manage is the SQLite log, which stores full prompt and response content and therefore constitutes a copy of whatever documents you processed.
alternatives: Direct HTTP calls to a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint, without the logging benefit
LangChain where provider abstraction inside an application matters more than shell composition
Ollama's own CLI for simple interactive use

name: Ragas
purpose: Evaluation framework for retrieval-augmented generation measuring faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision and recall, with synthetic test-set generation and support for custom metrics.
journalism_use_case: Answering the question an editor should ask before any AI document tool is trusted: how often does it produce an answer unsupported by the retrieved documents? Ragas' faithfulness metric measures exactly that, which is the difference between deploying a RAG system on evidence and on hope.
pros: Faithfulness measurement addresses the specific failure that matters in journalism — an answer not supported by the source — rather than general quality, so the metric maps onto editorial risk
Synthetic test-set generation lowers the barrier to having any evaluation at all, which most deployments skip entirely
Apache-2.0 with active maintenance (v0.4.4, 2026-11-14; pushed 2026-11-14) and substantial adoption (16,354 stars)
Transfer verified this session: explodinggradients/ragas now redirects to vibrantlabsai/ragas, so the canonical path is current
cons: Most metrics use a language model as judge, so you are evaluating one model's output with another model's judgement — useful as a relative signal, weak as an absolute measure, and this is routinely over-interpreted
Governance moved to a company (transfer verified 2026-11-17), which is a direction-and-continuity item to monitor for a project you would depend on for assurance
Synthetic test sets are generated from your documents by a model, so they inherit its blind spots; a human-written evaluation set from real reporting questions is substantially better
Running evaluation costs inference, and a thorough evaluation over a large corpus is a real compute expense
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 16,354 stars, release v0.4.4 (2026-11-14), pushed the same day, Apache-2.0; the repository transfer explodinggradients/ragas → vibrantlabsai/ragas was confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17 and recorded in leads.md L10.
assessment: Adopt the practice of measuring faithfulness before trusting any RAG system, and use Ragas as the convenient way to do it — while building a human-written evaluation set from your own reporting questions as the authoritative measure. For your profile the number worth putting in front of an editor is the faithfulness rate on your own corpus: if the system produces unsupported answers in a meaningful fraction of cases, that is a reason to restrict it to retrieval-with-citations rather than generated answers.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v0.4.4 published the same day, 16,354 stars, Apache-2.0, with the organisation transfer confirmed by redirect. Active releases; the governance change is the item to watch.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the library; judge models carry their own terms and costs.
licence_restrictions: None material. Note the organisation transfer when recording provenance.
costs: Library free. Evaluation consumes model inference — with a local model this is GPU time, with a hosted judge it is per-token charges (not priced here). A thorough evaluation of a large corpus is a real expense. Estimate.
privacy: Depends on the judge model: a local judge keeps your documents and answers internal, a hosted judge sends both to that provider — which for source material would be a serious disclosure made in the name of quality assurance.
alternatives: A hand-written evaluation set with manual scoring, which is more laborious and more trustworthy
promptfoo for broader prompt and model comparison
DeepEval as an alternative evaluation framework
blockers: LLM-as-judge metrics are relative signals, not absolute measures; a hosted judge would disclose source documents

name: promptfoo
purpose: Command-line and library tool for evaluating and comparing prompts, models and RAG configurations against test cases, with assertion types, side-by-side comparison and red-teaming for safety and prompt-injection testing.
journalism_use_case: Deciding which model and prompt to use, with evidence: run the same set of real newsroom tasks across several local models and prompt variants and compare outputs side by side — rather than choosing a model because it was in the news. The prompt-injection testing is separately valuable when documents come from hostile sources.
pros: Side-by-side comparison across models and prompts on your own tasks is exactly how this decision should be made, and almost nobody does it — this makes it cheap enough to actually do
Prompt-injection and red-teaming features address a genuine newsroom threat: a leaked document containing instructions aimed at your AI pipeline is a realistic attack, and testing for it is prudent
MIT licensed with very active maintenance (0.125.1, 2026-10-25; pushed 2026-11-17) and strong adoption (27,370 stars)
Configuration-as-YAML means an evaluation is a version-controlled artefact you can rerun when a model changes
cons: Assertion design is where the work is: a weak test set produces a confident wrong conclusion about which model is better, and the tool cannot supply domain judgement
Commercial company with an enterprise offering, so some features and the hosted path are paid — check the boundary before depending on something
Evaluation runs cost inference, and comparing several models across many cases multiplies that
Red-teaming output needs interpretation: a model that fails an injection test may still be fine behind proper input handling, and vice versa
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 27,370 stars with release 0.125.1 (2026-10-25), pushed 2026-11-17, MIT licence. Strong adoption is evident; the enterprise offering is documented by the vendor.
assessment: Adopt it for two specific decisions: which local model to standardise on, and whether your document-processing prompts are vulnerable to injection from hostile source material. For your profile the prompt-injection angle deserves emphasis — a newsroom pipeline that summarises documents from unknown sources is a realistic injection target, and a document instructing your model to exfiltrate or misreport is a plausible attack that nobody tests for. Build the evaluation set from real tasks.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 0.125.1 (2026-10-25), 27,370 stars, MIT licence. Same-day commits with a frequent release cadence under commercial maintenance.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the tool; evaluated models carry their own terms.
licence_restrictions: None material for the open tool. Enterprise features and hosted services are separate commercial offerings.
costs: Tool free. Evaluation consumes inference across every model and case combination — the main cost, and it scales multiplicatively. Local models make it a GPU-time expense rather than a per-token one. Estimate.
privacy: Evaluations run against whichever models you configure; using hosted providers sends your test cases (which may contain real document content) to them. Build evaluation sets from non-sensitive material, or use local models only.
alternatives: Ragas for RAG-specific faithfulness metrics
Inspect AI for a more rigorous evaluation framework
Manual side-by-side review of a dozen real cases, which is cruder and often sufficient to make the decision

name: Inspect AI
purpose: Framework for large language model evaluations with datasets, solvers, scorers and a log viewer, designed for rigorous and reproducible evaluation including multi-turn and tool-use tasks.
journalism_use_case: Building a defensible evaluation of whether a model is fit for an editorial task: a structured, reproducible evaluation with a viewable log of every sample, which is what you want when the question 'can we trust this for fact-checking support' has to be answered to an editor rather than asserted.
pros: Built by a government AI-safety institute for rigorous evaluation, so the design prioritises reproducibility and auditability over convenience — which is the right priority for a journalism assurance question
The log viewer makes every sample inspectable, so you can read the actual failures rather than only a score, and failures are where the editorial judgement lives
MIT licensed with very active maintenance (0.3.290, 2026-11-14; pushed 2026-11-17) and institutional backing
Supports tool use and multi-turn evaluation, so agentic workflows can be evaluated rather than only single prompts
cons: Smaller community than promptfoo (3,276 stars) and oriented to AI-safety research conventions, so there is less newsroom-adjacent material and more conceptual overhead
Rigour costs effort: defining datasets, solvers and scorers properly is a project, not an afternoon, and a half-built Inspect evaluation is no better than a quick promptfoo comparison
Very high release number with frequent releases, so pinning is essential
Evaluation inference costs apply as with any evaluation framework
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,276 stars with release 0.3.290 (2026-11-14), pushed 2026-11-17, MIT licence, maintained by the UK AI Security Institute. The institutional provenance is unusual in this category and is the main reason to take it seriously despite the smaller community.
assessment: Worth adopting when an AI deployment decision needs to be defensible rather than merely informed — for example before placing a model anywhere near fact-checking or source-material triage. For your profile the practical split is promptfoo for quick comparative decisions and Inspect for the one or two evaluations you would want to show an editor, a funder or a court. The log viewer is the feature that makes an evaluation persuasive to a non-technical reader.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 0.3.290 (2026-11-14), 3,276 stars, MIT licence. Same-day commits with a very frequent release cadence under government-institute maintenance.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the framework; evaluated models carry their own terms.
costs: Framework free. Evaluation inference is the cost; rigorous evaluation over many samples is substantial. Local models convert this to GPU time. Estimate.
privacy: Runs against configured models; a local model keeps evaluation content internal. Logs contain full samples, so if your evaluation uses real document content the logs need protecting accordingly.
alternatives: promptfoo for faster, lighter comparative evaluation
Ragas for RAG-specific faithfulness metrics
lm-evaluation-harness for standard academic benchmarks, which are less relevant to newsroom tasks
